newsitem.title: USA: Clinton encouraged by Kremlin change before summit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton encouraged by Kremlin change before summit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday he was encouraged by Russian President Boris Yeltsin's latest Kremlin changes before the start of their two-day summit that starts on Thursday in Helsinki.

"I'm encouraged by the new economic theme President Yeltsin announced this week," Clinton said just hours before his departure for the summit. "It underscores Russia's commitment to continued reform."

Yeltsin in recent days has shaken up his Cabinet in a move intended, at least in part, to re-establish his authority after long illness and to bring market-oriented economic reformers into senior Cabinet positions.

Anatoly Chubais, a prominent reformer recently restored to power as a first deputy premier, said on Tuesday the radical reshuffle was not yet over. "There will be more surprises," he told commercial NTV television.

"Now, the challenge is to create a climate that actually attracts more investment and promotes more trade so that Russia will have real economic growth," said Clinton, adding that he and Yeltsin "will discuss the steps that both of us will take to create that climate."
Clinton met with senior advisers to study the implications of the changes before making his remarks to reporters at the White House.
The Finland summit also was expected to focus on Russia's opposition to NATO plans to expand its membership to include some of Moscow's onetime Warsaw Pact allies.

The president also crammed his last few hours of White House time with domestic politics, trying to break an impasse in talks with Republican congressional leaders on balancing the federal budget. Clinton also had more physical therapy for his injured right knee.
He underwent surgery last Friday to reattach a tendon torn from the knee when he caught his heel on a stair.
The Helsinki meeting marks the first personal encounter for the U.S. and Russian presidents since an April summit in Moscow.

Ironically, the Finnish city replaced Washington, the venue originally scheduled, in order to make the trip less arduous for Yeltsin, who had heart by-pass surgery late last year and has struggled with double pneumonia more recently.
While he has been looking more robust of late, Clinton has essentially been confined to a wheelchair.

Released from the hospital on Sunday, he was forced to delay the start of the summit by one day and cancel plans to visit Denmark despite initial vows that the injury would not affect his summit schedule.

Senior administration officials stressed that they expected no dramatic breakthroughs at the summit. Instead, they hope for progress in smoothing over divisive issues like the prospective NATO expansion and perhaps making some progress toward a charter spelling out NATO-Russia relations.
Washington also hopes to begin a new round of talks on nuclear missile reductions with Moscow, but first wants the Russian parliament to ratify the long-delayed START-2 treaty, signed in 1993.
